summary: Moclobemide is a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type A (RIMA) used to treat major depression and, in some countries, social anxiety disorder. By reversibly and selectively inhibiting MAO-A it reduces the metabolism of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine, increasing their synaptic availability. Because inhibition is reversible and short-lived, the interaction with dietary tyramine is much weaker than with irreversible MAOIs, so a strict low-tyramine diet is usually unnecessary, although large amounts of tyramine-rich food should still be avoided and the drug taken after meals. The usual adult dose is about 300 mg/day in divided doses (range 150-600 mg/day). Moclobemide is not FDA-approved; dosing follows the EMA/SmPC and BNF. It is contraindicated with other serotonergic agents (including SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, pethidine and other MAOIs) because of the risk of serotonin syndrome, and should be avoided in acute confusional states and phaeochromocytoma. Antidepressants carry a class warning of increased suicidal thinking in young people.

moa: Moclobemide is a reversible, selective inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type A (RIMA). MAO-A is the enzyme responsible for the oxidative deamination of serotonin, noradrenaline and (with MAO-B) dopamine. By reversibly binding MAO-A, moclobemide reduces the breakdown of these monoamine neurotransmitters and increases their concentration in the central nervous system, producing an antidepressant effect. Because the inhibition is reversible and the enzyme is quickly freed, ingested tyramine can still be metabolised and can also displace moclobemide from the enzyme, so the dietary tyramine ('cheese reaction') risk is much lower than with irreversible MAOIs.

absolute: Concurrent use with other MAOIs or serotonergic drugs (SSRIs/SNRIs, clomipramine, triptans, pethidine, dextromethorphan, selegiline) - serotonin syndrome risk
relative: Bipolar disorder (risk of switch to mania/agitation)
monitor: Mood, anxiety and suicidal ideation, especially early and in young patients
Signs of serotonin syndrome when other serotonergic drugs are involved

preg: There are limited data on moclobemide in pregnancy. Avoid use unless the expected benefit outweighs the potential risk, and consider better-characterised alternatives where appropriate.
lact: Only a small amount of moclobemide passes into breast milk. Avoid use during breastfeeding or use with caution if no suitable alternative is available, monitoring the infant.
renal: No specific dose reduction is generally required in renal impairment, as the active drug is extensively metabolised.
hepatic: Moclobemide is extensively metabolised by the liver. In severe hepatic impairment, or where metabolism is markedly inhibited (e.g. by cimetidine), the dose should be reduced to one-half or one-third of the usual dose.

major: Other MAOIs and serotonergic antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, clomipramine) - serotonin syndrome (contraindicated/avoid)
Pethidine and other opioids (dextromethorphan, tramadol) - serotonin syndrome / severe reactions
Sympathomimetics (incl. ephedrine, pseudoephedrine) - enhanced pressor effect
moderate: Cimetidine - inhibits moclobemide metabolism; reduce moclobemide dose
Selegiline - increased risk of hypertensive reactions/serotonin syndrome
interactions.food: Avoid large amounts of tyramine-rich foods (mature cheese, fermented/cured products, yeast extracts); take after food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive sedation; some alcoholic drinks contain tyramine
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference; monitor blood pressure clinically

Suicidal ideation/behaviour, particularly in young adults
Switch to mania/hypomania in susceptible patients
emergency: Serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental state)

Signs of serotonin syndrome when co-administered serotonergic drugs cannot be avoided

counsel: This medicine treats depression by increasing brain chemicals; it may take 1-2 weeks or more to feel the benefit
Take it after food; you do not need a strict diet, but avoid large amounts of mature cheese, cured/fermented foods and yeast extracts
Avoid other antidepressants, certain painkillers (pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan), migraine triptans and cold/flu decongestants unless your doctor approves
Seek urgent help for high fever with stiffness, agitation and sweating, or for severe headache
Tell your doctor if mood worsens or you have thoughts of self-harm, and do not stop the medicine suddenly without advice
pk: Antidepressant effect develops over 1-3 weeks; enzyme inhibition is immediate
Plasma peak about 1-2 hours after an oral dose
Short - elimination half-life about 1-4 hours (MAO-A inhibition is reversible and short-lived)
Because inhibition is reversible, enzyme activity recovers within about 24 hours of stopping
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from moisture
pearls: RIMA - reversible, selective MAO-A inhibitor; much lower dietary tyramine ('cheese reaction') risk than irreversible MAOIs, but avoid large tyramine loads
Serotonin syndrome is the key danger - avoid SSRIs/SNRIs, pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, triptans and other MAOIs
Short half-life and reversible inhibition mean rapid offset (about 24 h) - useful when switching antidepressants with appropriate washout
Take after food; reduce the dose with cimetidine or severe hepatic impairment
Not FDA-approved; dosing per EMA/SmPC and BNF. Antidepressant class warning of suicidality in young people
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose. Do not double up. Because the drug is short-acting, try to keep to your usual schedule.
overdose: Overdose is usually of low toxicity when taken alone, causing agitation, aggression, drowsiness, disorientation and gastrointestinal symptoms. Combined overdose with serotonergic drugs greatly increases the risk of serious serotonin syndrome. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring of vital signs and temperature; treat serotonin syndrome with cooling, benzodiazepines and supportive care.
